sections.content:
You know the future and conditional of probability from B1 Unit 22 (*Estará en casa*, *Serían las ocho*). Here, the same two tenses do a different job: they concede a point before a *pero* clause that limits or outweighs it.

In conversation and opinion writing, the **simple future** concedes a present or general point (*Será caro, pero vale la pena* = "It may well be expensive, but it is worth it"). The **simple conditional** concedes a past point (*Tendría razón, pero no supo explicarlo* = "He may well have been right, but he could not explain it"). Without the *pero* clause (or an equivalent contrast such as *sin embargo*), the verb reads as probability rather than concession.

When the conceded event is already completed before the present, speakers also use the **future perfect** (*Habrá costado mucho, pero funciona bien*); for a completed past concession before another past point, the **conditional perfect** (*Habría sido un lujo, pero nadie protestó*). This concessive use is natural in both spoken Spanish and columns.

sections.title: Concessive future and conditional
rows: *Será costoso, pero compensa.* (It may well be costly, but it pays off.)
*Tendría defectos, pero cumplió su función.* (It may well have had flaws, but it did its job.)
*Habrá sido exagerado, pero logró su objetivo.* (It may well have been over the top, but it achieved its goal.)
*Habría parecido un lujo, pero era necesario.* (It might have seemed a luxury, but it was necessary.)

items.spanish: Será un poco costoso, pero vale la pena por la calidad.
items.english: It may well be a bit costly, but it is worth it for the quality.

items.spanish: Tendría razón en su crítica, pero el tono fue exagerado.
items.english: He may well have been right in his criticism, but the tone was over the top.

items.spanish: Habrá tenido algún defecto al principio, pero el resultado final compensa.
items.english: It may well have had some flaw at the start, but the final result makes up for it.

items.spanish: Será un lujo para algunos, pero no es para tanto si se usa todos los días.
items.english: It may well be a luxury for some, but it is no big deal if it is used every day.

sections.content: English speakers often translate "It may be expensive, but..." with *Puede que sea caro, pero...*, which is grammatical but longer. Spanish prefers the compact concessive future (*Será caro, pero...*) and always pairs it with a contrast clause (*pero*, *sin embargo*) so the listener hears a concession rather than a guess.
